title: Cedar Fulfillment POC — synthetic burst & steady-state inference econ scan
body:
Summary:

This note captures the benchmarking and performance-economics scan we ran for the Cedar Fulfillment POC (internal name: CEDAR-F). Objective was to understand: (1) whether Redwood can meet a 150ms p95 LLM generate SLO for short-form responses (avg 60 tokens) at 200 qps steady-state, (2) how headroom and cost behave under short microbursts (1–3s spikes to 1.2k qps), and (3) which serving knobs (batch sizes, quantization profile, routing to cheaper variants) give the best unit-economics without breaking the SLO.

Key conclusions (top-line):
- Baseline (float16, model v1.0 on A100-equivalent hosts): meets 150ms p95 at up to ~220 qps steady-state with 8-instance pool, p99 grows sharply beyond 180 qps.
- Microburst behavior: cold-start-like microbursts (spikes from 200->1200 qps over <2s) produce tail amplification: p99 for affected requests rose to 1.1s; overall error budget risk if bursts are common.
- Cost vs performance: switching to the int8-quantized profile reduces per-1M-token inference cost by ~28% while increasing median latency by ~12ms and p95 by ~18ms. Combined with adaptive routing to a slightly cheaper model variant for low-risk paths, total cost reductions of 35% are achievable with <10% SLO risk for non-critical endpoints.
- Recommended deployment: start with a hybrid pool (6 float16 nodes + 4 int8 nodes) with routing policy: prefer int8 for non-critical, fallback to float16 on latency slip; enable prefix caching and 3s request coalescing window to reduce microburst amplification.

Methodology and test harness:
- Synthetic workload constructed from Cedar production logs (sanitized) and augmented with synthetic microburst generator to control ramp profiles. Workload mixes: 70% short-chat (30–90 tokens), 20% single-turn completion (10–30 tokens), 10% multi-part (200+ tokens).
- Core metrics: qps, p50/p95/p99 generation latency (end-to-end, server-side), token throughput (tokens/sec per GPU), tail token amplification (extra tokens generated per cold-start), and dollars per 1M tokens (using internal cost model: instance-hour + GPU amortization + electricity + infra overhead).
- Environments: Hosted-equivalent cluster (A100 class), Dedicated small pool (NVIDIA H100 quantized), and a simulated Private VPC config (same hosts but with network emulation to mimic 60–80ms customer-side network).
- Runs: steady-state sweeps (50–350 qps), microburst sweeps (200qps baseline with spikes to 400/800/1200 qps with 0.5s/1s/3s durations), and failure-injection (GPU OOMs, node drain) to observe graceful degradation. Each datapoint is the aggregation of 3 x 10-minute runs; reported values are medians across runs.

Important raw numbers (selected):
- Baseline float16 (8-node pool):
  - 200 qps steady: p50 32ms, p95 118ms, p99 210ms, tokens/sec/GPU 1,900
  - 300 qps steady: p50 46ms, p95 176ms, p99 420ms (p99 increases non-linearly)
  - Cost: $9.8 per 1M tokens

- Int8-quantized profile (10-node pool):
  - 200 qps steady: p50 44ms, p95 136ms, p99 255ms, tokens/sec/GPU 2,400
  - 300 qps steady: p50 62ms, p95 210ms, p99 520ms
  - Cost: $7.1 per 1M tokens (28% lower than baseline)

- Hybrid (6 float16 + 4 int8) with adaptive routing:
  - Effective observed at 200 qps: p95 126ms, p99 230ms, blended cost: $6.9 per 1M tokens (includes routing overhead and cache benefits)
  - Observed SLO violations concentrated in 4% of requests (multi-part) where fallback to float16 occurred during capacity pressure.

Microburst findings (200->1200 qps ramp in 1s):
- Float16 pool: p99 for the burst window spikes to ~1.1s and queueing causes extra latency for co-batched sessions. Recovery to baseline p95 takes ~7–9s as the autoscaler adds capacity (policy: 30s cooldown).
- Int8 pool: higher throughput reduces immediate queuing; p99 peaks at ~720ms but overall more model error instances (minor hallucination rate increased by ~0.4% in the quantized model for a small subset of prompts).
- Mitigation experiments: enabling prefix KV caching reduced p95 tail amplification by ~18% for repeated prefixes; reducing the autoscaler cooldown to 8s (with slightly more aggressive buffer capacity) cut recovery time to ~3–4s but increased idle cost by ~11%.

Quality tradeoffs observed:
- Int8 quantization introduced subtle truncation artifacts for long single-turn generations (200+ tokens) in ~0.6% of samples; for the Cedar use-case (mostly short replies) this was acceptable after targeted prompt-level post-processing filters.
- When routing reliability policy falls back from int8 to float16 during slippage, average error rate stays within product thresholds. We instrumented rerun heatmaps to validate that fallback events cluster on multi-part requests.

Operational recommendations for the POC:
1) Sizing: initial Dedicated allocation: 6 x float16 GPU nodes + 4 x int8 GPU nodes. Reserve an autoscale headroom of +35% to absorb 3s microbursts.
2) Routing policy: prefer int8 for endpoints labeled low-criticality; immediate fallback to float16 on measured p95 > 150ms for the route. Use token-budget thresholds to avoid routing expensive multi-turn sessions to int8.
3) Autoscaler tuning: cooldown 8s, scale step = +20% per event, keep minimal baseline instances to avoid cold-start amplification.
4) Caching: enable prefix KV caching and short-lived request coalescing (window 50–150ms) for similar prefixes. This reduced token load by ~7% in our synth workload.
5) Observability: add a per-route SLO dashboard (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec/GPU, routing decisions, quantization fallback count) and an alert when fallback ratio > 5% over 5 minutes.
6) Quality monitoring: add a small daily eval set of 200 prompts (client-provided) to validate quantization drift; trigger automatic rollback if quality delta > 1% across key metrics (BLEU/ROUGE-like proxy + classifier-based acceptability).

Rollout plan for customer workshop:
- Week 0 (this week): share this note + runbook; schedule a 90-minute workshop with Cedar infra and application owners.
- Week 1: deploy hybrid pool to Dedicated environment, run live replay for an hour (both steady and 2x burst scenarios), collect observability traces.
- Week 2: iterate routing rules, tune autoscaler; rerun microburst suite; document residual risks.
- Acceptance criteria: sustained p95 < 150ms for 30m at 200 qps; successful handling of a 3s 1k-qps microburst with p99 < 800ms and no service errors.

Open questions and follow-ups (for workshop):
- Cedar must confirm which endpoints are truly SLO-critical vs. cheap-fallback candidates. We need a short mapping table.
- Confirm acceptable quality delta for int8 on multi-turns (is 0.6% regressions acceptable?).
- Decide on autoscaler cost tolerance (what incremental cost % is acceptable for faster cooldowns).

Appendix: quick-run checklist for solutions engineers during customer session:
- Pre-check: load customer sample traces into harness, validate token distribution matches our synthetic mix.
- Deploy hybrid pool (6f16 + 4i8) with smaller test traffic.
- Run steady sweep (200qps -> 300qps) for 10 minutes each.
- Run microburst sweep: 200->1.2k qps with 1s ramps, three repeats.
- Capture traces with route decision flags and quantization tag.
- Review p95/p99 and fallback counts; take snapshots of any prompt-level quality regressions.

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Look into integrating dynamic kv caching TTLs per-route (idea: longer for catalog-like prefixes, short for user-chat).
- Add a quick script to compute blended cost when varying int8 node ratios (input: node mix, qps mix) so PMs can fiddle during workshop.
- Circle back with Research on retraining/quantization-aware finetune for the few prompts that exhibit artifacts.
